candidateRows: Paul consistently understood Jesus as a physical Jewish man who died by Roman crucifixion and was later regarded as the resurrected Messiah.
Paul is the earliest evidence discussed, so Boyce's claim that Paul already believed in an earthly, bodily Jesus directly supports historicity against the celestial-Christ hypothesis.

Boyce appeals to Paul's activity before and after conversion, Paul's descriptions of death, burial, crucifixion, Abrahamic descent, birth from a woman, and the resurrection as the change in Paul's evaluation of Jesus.
Paul's designation of James as the brother of the Lord identifies a particular biological relative of Jesus rather than merely a fellow Christian.
A biological brother personally encountered by Paul would be strong early evidence that Jesus was an earthly person and would directly undermine a wholly celestial origin account.

Boyce argues that common names required distinguishing descriptions, compares Paul's naming of Cephas and James, and maintains that a generic Christian-brother reading would increase rather than resolve ambiguity.
Josephus and other ancient writers used relational and titular descriptions to identify real people, supporting the biological reading of James as Jesus's brother.
The argument supplies external linguistic and historical corroboration for Boyce's identification of James and Jesus, extending his case beyond an isolated interpretation of Paul.

Boyce invokes Josephus's description of James and Jesus, naming conventions in other writings, and Roman references to Christianity to argue that family connections, locations, and titles identified persons of interest.
Hegesippus preserves a traceable dynasty of Jesus's physical relatives who led the Jerusalem church into the early second century.
A continuing family line attached to Jesus and early Jerusalem leadership would directly establish an earthly man with physical relatives remembered across generations.

Boyce cites traditions about Jude's grandchildren, imperial questioning of Jesus's relatives, and a succession of family leadership ending around 110 CE, then infers that Jesus was a real man with traceable relatives.
Jesus belongs to a wider class of suffering savior lords treated as historical despite being mythical, so his historicity requires exceptional evidence.

This establishes Carrier's central comparative prior: Christianity resembles other savior cults whose heroes did not exist, shifting the case toward requiring affirmative evidence for Jesus as an exception.

Carrier compares Jesus with numerous ancient savior figures whose suffering defeated death and promised followers a blessed afterlife, arguing that similar narrative and cultic features do not establish a historical founder.
The earliest writings locate knowledge of Jesus in scripture and revelation, while their apparent references to birth and brothers remain allegorical or ambiguous.

If the earliest sources never clearly place Jesus on earth or identify witnesses and biological relations, their evidentiary pattern supports Carrier's celestial-origin hypothesis over straightforward historicity.

Carrier argues that Paul received information through scripture and revelation, never mentions earthly disciples, treats being born of a woman within allegory, and uses brother language broadly enough to leave biological kinship uncertain.
The Gospels are late, anonymous, unsourced, mythically structured accounts whose claims receive no demonstrably independent historical corroboration.

Carrier's overall conclusion depends on denying that the later narrative and historical sources independently establish Jesus, leaving no evidence sufficient to distinguish him from other mythical savior figures.

Carrier characterizes the Gospels as anonymous works written later in another language and land, argues that later historians relied on Gospel traditions or Christian informants, and concludes that this cannot independently establish Jesus.
Paul could believe Jesus possessed Jewish and Davidic flesh, died, and rose while still placing those events in a celestial drama known only through scripture and revelation.

The clarification answers the historicist inference from bodily language by separating material embodiment from earthly location, preserving the celestial hypothesis despite Paul's references to flesh, death, and resurrection.
Boyce's opening treated Paul's references to flesh, crucifixion, burial, and resurrection as evidence that Paul believed in an earthly historical Jesus.

Carrier concedes several descriptions emphasized by Boyce but argues that Paul never locates the events on earth, attributes death and resurrection knowledge to scripture, and describes apostolic encounters only after resurrection.
The grammar and argumentative context of Galatians leave James's title brother of the Lord ambiguous and do not establish that he was Jesus's biological brother.
Boyce makes James a principal early witness to Jesus's physical family, so preserving a non-biological reading removes one of the historicity case's most important Pauline anchors.
Boyce argued that Paul named James as brother of the Lord specifically to distinguish Jesus's biological relative from other men named James.

Carrier argues that Paul's Greek excludes James from the apostles in the immediate statement, says Paul names everyone he met to defend his independence, and concludes that the title could denote either biological kinship or a Christian category.
The gospels resemble invented narratives about other savior figures, lack checkable sourcing, and therefore cannot reliably establish a historical Jesus.
This directly challenges a principal class of evidence for historicity by arguing that the gospel narratives are unsourced, myth-like, and historically unverifiable.
The historicity defense's reliance on gospel narratives as evidence for an earthly Jesus.
Carrier argues that the foreign-language, unsourced gospels resemble fabricated biographies of savior heroes and Moses, while later believers provide no access to their original sources.
Paul's allegorical discussion in Galatians culminates in the literal event of God's son being born of a woman in the fullness of time.
The move treats a disputed Pauline passage as affirmative evidence that Jesus entered history through an actual human birth rather than only a celestial event.
Carrier's contention that Paul's language about Abrahamic descent and birth is allegorical rather than biographical.
Boyce accepts that Paul employs allegory but argues that its application has literal effects and reaches consummation when God sends his son, born of a woman.
Paul's repeated references identify the James in Galatians as the same specific church leader rather than an otherwise incidental baptized Christian.
Identifying James as a particular leading associate and brother of the Lord bears directly on whether Paul knew people personally connected to a historical Jesus.
Carrier's interpretation of James, brother of the Lord, as an incidental rank-and-file Christian rather than Jesus's relative.
Boyce argues that Galatians establishes James's identity once and then repeats his name among the pillars, following a normal practice for distinguishing people with common names.
Tacitus likely obtained the time, ruler, and execution details for Christianity's origin from Roman archival records rather than Christian rumor.

Carrier's claim that Tacitus lacked an independent early source and probably obtained his information from Christians.

Boyce's argument that Galatians moves from allegory to a literal earthly birth of Jesus in the fullness of time.
Carrier says Paul knows a recent incarnation but cites only revelation and scripture, then reads the women, birth, and law language through the Sarah-and-Hagar allegorical structure.
The grammar and differing descriptions in Galatians distinguish the non-apostle James of chapter one from the apostolic pillar James of chapter two.
The distinction removes the asserted identification of Paul's James as a leading eyewitness or biological relative and weakens a major Pauline historicity argument.
Boyce's claim that Paul's repeated use of James identifies one person already established as the brother of the Lord.
Carrier argues that Paul labels the chapter-two James as a pillar, while the chapter-one construction excludes its James from the apostles and mentions him only for completeness.
Hegesippus supplies no identifiable or checked sources, and his implausible James narrative reflects selective preservation of Christian propaganda rather than reliable history.
The move challenges whether later Christian historiography can corroborate Jesus or his associates by attacking both source transparency and the preservation process.
Boyce's presentation of Hegesippus and later preservation of his reports as historically accountable testimony derived from early churches.
Carrier characterizes the James story as apocryphal and implausible, stresses that Hegesippus names no sources or checks, and argues that favorable Christian selectors preserved it.
Tacitus lacked an early archival source for Christ's execution because Pliny the Younger, despite mastering Pliny the Elder's work, knew no such account.
The argument seeks to disqualify Tacitus as independent non-Christian corroboration by testing the proposed archival pathway against the Plinys' surviving correspondence and knowledge.
Boyce's contention that Tacitus probably used Roman archives to locate Christ's execution under Pilate and Tiberius.
Carrier identifies Pliny the Elder as Tacitus's likely Neronian source, then infers that it contained no execution report because Pliny the Younger did not know it.
A Messiah capable of persuading Jews through the Torah and prophets had to be physically born as an Abrahamic and Davidic Jew who fulfilled the law.
The argument directly supports an earthly historical Jesus by claiming that the earliest Jewish and Gentile conversions required a physically born, crucified Jewish Messiah.
Carrier's reading of Paul's Galatians argument as compatible with a celestial incarnation rather than a physical Jewish birth.
Boyce argues that Paul's audience required substantial scriptural evidence and would not abandon prior gods for a Messiah lacking physical Jewish descent, death, and eyewitness reports.
Neither the unspecified James appearance nor the disputed Galatians grammar establishes a biological brother, while Greek usage supports treating James as a non-apostle.
This answers a major proposed personal link between Paul and a historical Jesus by denying both the biological identification and the grammatical inference supporting it.
Boyce's renewed argument that the named James is a distinct Jerusalem eyewitness and that the grammar includes him among the apostles.

Carrier says Paul never calls the appearance recipient Jesus's biological brother, treats acknowledged grammatical dispute as unusable support, and appeals to comparative Greek constructions and pillar terminology.
Acts shows no concern about Jesus's missing body and contradicts Paul's own account, so it cannot reliably establish the earliest Christian history.
The reliability of Acts directly affects whether its earthly narrative can outweigh Paul's earlier testimony when reconstructing Christian origins.
The historicist appeal to Acts as evidence for an earthly body and for Paul's participation in events surrounding Stephen.
Carrier argues that Acts never explains the body's fate, centers Paul's conversion on a vision, and places Paul at Stephen's death despite Paul's contrary account in Galatians.
Paul's references to an actual death and burial remain compatible with a celestial Christ because ancient Jews envisioned material counterparts and burial places in heaven.
This addresses whether Paul's death-and-burial language necessarily locates Jesus on Earth, a decisive point separating historicity from mythicism.
The historicist contention that Paul's statement that Christ died and was buried entails an earthly human Jesus.
Carrier accepts that Paul meant a real death and burial but argues that contemporary cosmology populated heavenly levels with gardens, structures, and physical counterparts capable of hosting burial.
Galatians 4 uses birth from a woman allegorically, while Romans 1 may envision Jesus's Davidic flesh being divinely made directly from Davidic seed rather than ordinary descent.
These Pauline phrases are central historicist evidence for ordinary human birth and ancestry, so an alternative reading bears directly on the motion.
The historicist use of Paul's woman-born and Davidic-seed language as evidence of ordinary human birth and biological ancestry.

Carrier distinguishes physical Davidic flesh from normal genealogy, reads the Nathan prophecy literally as direct manufacture from David's seed, and treats Galatians 4's woman language as part of Paul's allegory.
Luke's historical framing and claimed receipt of prior information make Luke-Acts an independent source rather than merely dependent narrative material.
Whether Luke-Acts supplies independent historical attestation materially affects the cumulative evidence for an earthly Jesus and early Christian events.
Carrier's dismissal of Luke-Acts as late, dependent, and unreliable evidence for reconstructing the earliest Christian movement.
Boyce points to the historical character of Luke's opening and its claim to received information, asking why the work should not count as an independent source despite common authorship with Acts.

Luke imitates the appearance of history but withholds identifiable sources, rewrites earlier gospels, and inserts Christian figures into borrowed historical material rather than independently corroborating them.
The argument challenges the independence and evidentiary value of a major narrative source used to support an earthly Jesus and apostolic history.
Boyce's claim that Luke's historical presentation and professed access to earlier information make Luke-Acts an independent source.

Carrier argues that Luke borrows historiographic conventions without the source disclosure found in genuine histories, depends on Mark and Matthew, and uses Josephus-like background material without corroborating Christian claims.
Attaching the description brother of the Lord to the common personal name James functions as a specific identifier and therefore points to a biological relationship.
If Paul identifies James as Jesus's biological brother, the passage supplies direct early evidence that Jesus was a historical human person.
Carrier's interpretation of James as merely a cultic Christian brother rather than a biological brother of Jesus.

Boyce argues that Paul needed to identify the additional person he met, that kinship descriptions ordinarily distinguish people with common names, and that treating this instance generically would be exceptional.
Because Paul calls baptized Christians brothers of Jesus, the unqualified phrase brother of the Lord cannot by itself specify that James was Jesus's biological sibling.
The meaning of Paul's designation for James is one of the debate's principal pieces of early evidence for or against a historical Jesus.
Boyce's argument that a kinship description attached to James's personal name must distinguish a biological brother.
Carrier maintains that Paul routinely uses fictive kinship, never expressly identifies biological brothers of Jesus, and expands the phrase only when distinguishing ordinary Christians from apostles.
Although sibling terminology can denote a general religious group, its attachment to an individual name ordinarily provides specific identification, as parallel naming practices illustrate.
The proposed naming convention supports the biological reading of James's title and thus strengthens early Pauline evidence for Jesus's human family.
Carrier's claim that Paul's fictive sibling terminology makes the designation attached to James insufficient to indicate biological kinship.

Boyce concedes generic uses of brother language but distinguishes constructions attached to personal names, illustrating how ancient writers used added descriptions to disambiguate people sharing common names.
Analogies to ordinary named brothers fail because only Jesus had an established class of cultic brothers, creating an ambiguity that Paul would have needed to resolve explicitly to mean biology.
The distinction supplies Carrier's principal reason for denying that conventional kinship identifiers establish James as the biological brother of Jesus.
Boyce's comparison of James brother of the Lord with naming constructions used to identify biological brothers of other named individuals.

Carrier argues that examples involving the sons of Zebedee are inapposite because no cultic brotherhood existed around them, whereas Paul's audience already knew Christians as adopted brothers of Jesus.
Paul's use of familial language for named associates such as Phoebe shows that individual kinship descriptions can be specific even within a broader practice of fictive family terminology.
The examples test Carrier's proposed linguistic distinction and support Boyce's broader case that the wording attached to James is individually identifying.
Carrier's claim that the established cultic brotherhood of Jesus makes other ancient biological-brother naming analogies inapplicable.
Boyce invokes Paul's descriptions of Phoebe, Timothy, and Titus to argue that Paul regularly applies family terminology to particular named individuals, not solely to undifferentiated groups.
The phrase concerning brothers of the Lord can denote blood relationship, especially when a personal name requires clarification.
Whether James is identified as Jesus's biological brother is a central piece of Pauline evidence for a historical earthly Jesus.
Carrier's claim that Pauline brother language normally denotes a cultic rather than biological relationship.
After locating 1 Corinthians 9:5, Boyce distinguishes Jewish, communal, and blood-related senses of brother language and stresses clarification attached to personal names.
Because Paul says baptized Christians are adopted by God as Jesus's brothers, Galatians 1 needed an explicit biological qualifier to identify James as a blood brother.
The argument directly contests one of the principal Pauline passages used to establish that Jesus had a biological family and therefore existed historically.
Boyce's argument that attaching brother-of-the-Lord language to the personal name James naturally clarifies a biological relationship.

Carrier grants the proposed naming convention in ordinary cases but argues Christianity's explicit fictive brotherhood makes Jesus exceptional and renders the Galatians wording insufficiently specific.
Acts can identify James as the Lord's brother without adding an in-the-flesh qualifier because the biological sense is supplied contextually.
This challenges Carrier's linguistic test for biological kinship and supports reading comparable brother terminology as evidence of Jesus's family.
Carrier's claim that a biological brother of Jesus would need to be explicitly identified with an in-the-flesh qualification.
Boyce argues that excessive specificity can itself create clarity and appeals to the treatment of James in Acts as evidence that context can establish physical kinship.
References to James and John in Acts do not resolve the Lord's-brother phrase because only Jesus has both adopted and purported biological categories of brothers.
The distinction is offered to preserve the cultic reading of James in Paul against a major historicist analogy drawn from Acts.
Boyce's appeal to Acts as showing that brother terminology can identify physical kinship without an explicit fleshly qualifier.

Carrier argues that brother of John has only a biological reading, whereas brother of the Lord is ambiguous because Paul explicitly recognizes adopted brothers of Jesus but never clearly biological ones.
Tacitus neither claims nor was likely able to consult Roman execution records for Jesus, so his information cannot be treated as archival confirmation.

Boyce's suggestion that Tacitus may have traced Christian origins through court records available to him in Rome.

Carrier denies that the relevant passage names records, argues Jerusalem executions were not archived through a later bureaucratic system, and says surviving Roman materials would not establish such access.

Boyce's contention that Tacitus's account may rest on documentary or investigative tracing rather than Christian reports.
Carrier uses Pliny's admitted questioning of Christians and his communication with Tacitus to argue that an independent source is speculative and cannot serve as a historical premise.
Jesus resembles other historicized mythical heroes, while Paul lacks an earthly biography and the later Gospels and historians provide no demonstrably independent evidence.
The synthesis states the overarching mythicist case: prior plausibility from comparable myths combines with weak, late, dependent, and nonbiographical evidence.

Carrier compares Jesus with invented savior figures, emphasizes Paul's silence about an earthly ministry, characterizes the Gospels as late literary elaborations, and denies independence to later historians.
Paul's Pharisaic background, persecution mission, and transformative Damascus experience support his belief that a real executed Jesus rose bodily from death.

Common Palestinian names required identifying descriptors, so Paul's designation of James as the Lord's brother follows a normal pattern for distinguishing a specific individual.
